chunks: And that which was narrated is: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Muhammad ibn Humran from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

He said: 'Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) forbade keeping the meat of sacrificial animals for more than three days.' This is not contradictory to the first report because it is not impossible that Muhammad ibn Muslim shared hearing the report with Abu al-Subbah, and that the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) forbade that, then said, then permitted eating it afterwards, so Muhammad ibn Muslim forgot it, while Abu al-Subbah narrated it. And if it were not so, it would be understood that it is preferable not to do [keep it] after the three days, and that what remains is best to be given in charity, and it is permissible for the meat of the sacrifices to be taken out of Mina.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on keeping sacrificial meat for more than three days in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi presents this narration from Imam al-Sadiq to resolve the apparent contradiction between the prohibition of storing sacrificial meat and the practice of keeping it for extended periods, suggesting the initial ban was abrogated or forgotten by some narrators like Muhammad ibn Muslim. The text clarifies that while consuming the meat after three days is permissible, it is preferable (mustahabb) to distribute it in charity, and it explicitly permits transporting the meat out of Mina, a detail often debated in fiqh. This reflects the Shia methodology of harmonizing conflicting reports through temporal sequencing or abrogation rather than dismissing one as weak.
